meta.title: Complex Analysis I — Module I: Complex Numbers, the Complex Plane and Polar Form
meta.subject: Complex Analysis I (MAT5CJ303, Sem 5)

glossary.definition: The imaginary unit is the number \(i\) defined by the property that its square is negative one, \(i^2 = -1\).
A complex number is any number of the form \(z = a + ib\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers and \(i\) is the imaginary unit.
glossary.example: In Definition 1.1.1, \(z = 4 - 9i\) is a complex number with \(a = 4\) and \(b = -9\).

glossary.definition: In \(z = a + ib\), the real number \(a = \text{Re}(z)\) is the real part, the real number \(b = \text{Im}(z)\) is the imaginary part, and \(ib\) (when \(a = 0\)) is a pure imaginary number.
glossary.example: For \(z = 4 - 9i\), \(\text{Re}(z) = 4\) and \(\text{Im}(z) = -9\) (not \(-9i\)); \(z = 6i\) is pure imaginary.

glossary.definition: Two complex numbers \(z_1 = a_1 + ib_1\) and \(z_2 = a_2 + ib_2\) are equal, \(z_1 = z_2\), if and only if \(a_1 = a_2\) and \(b_1 = b_2\).
glossary.example: By Definition 1.1.2, \(z_1 = z_2\) means \(\text{Re}(z_1) = \text{Re}(z_2)\) and \(\text{Im}(z_1) = \text{Im}(z_2)\).

glossary.definition: The complex conjugate of \(z = a + ib\), written \(\bar{z}\), is the complex number \(\bar{z} = a - ib\) obtained by changing the sign of the imaginary part.
For a nonzero complex number \(z\), the multiplicative inverse (or reciprocal) is the unique number \(z^{-1} = 1/z\) such that \(zz^{-1} = 1\), while \(-z = -a - ib\) is the additive inverse.
glossary.example: In Example 3 of §1.1, the reciprocal of \(z = 2 - 3i\) is \(z^{-1} = \frac{2}{13} + \frac{3}{13}i\).

glossary.definition: The complex plane (or \(z\)-plane) is the coordinate plane in which \(z = x + iy\) is plotted as the point \((x, y)\), with the horizontal real axis and vertical imaginary axis.
glossary.example: The number \(z = 2 - 3i\) corresponds to the point \((2, -3)\) in the \(z\)-plane.

glossary.definition: The modulus (or absolute value) of a complex number \(z = x + iy\) is the nonnegative real number \(|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), equal to the distance from the origin to \((x, y)\).
The distance between two points \(z_1 = x_1 + iy_1\) and \(z_2 = x_2 + iy_2\) in the complex plane is \(|z_2 - z_1| = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\).
glossary.example: In Example 2 of §1.2, \(|z| = |z - i|\) means \(z\) is equidistant from \(0\) and \(i\).

glossary.definition: The triangle inequality states that for any two complex numbers \(z_1\) and \(z_2\), \(|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|\), with lower bound \(\big||z_1| - |z_2|\big| \le |z_1 + z_2|\).
glossary.example: Geometrically, the side \(z_1 + z_2\) of a vector triangle cannot exceed the sum of the other two sides.

glossary.definition: The polar form of a nonzero complex number \(z = x + iy\) is \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), where \(r = |z|\) is the modulus and \(\theta = \arg(z)\) is an argument of \(z\).
glossary.example: In Example 1 of §1.3, \(-\sqrt{3} - i = 2\left(\cos\frac{7\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)\).

glossary.definition: An argument of a nonzero complex number \(z = x + iy\), denoted \(\theta = \arg(z)\), is any radian angle of inclination from the positive real axis satisfying \(\cos\theta = x/r\) and \(\sin\theta = y/r\).
glossary.example: Because sine and cosine have period \(2\pi\), if \(\theta_0\) is an argument of \(z\), then \(\theta_0 \pm 2n\pi\) are also arguments.

glossary.definition: The principal argument of a nonzero complex number \(z\), denoted \(\text{Arg}(z)\), is the unique argument \(\theta\) of \(z\) that lies in the interval \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\).
glossary.example: For \(z = -\sqrt{3} - i\), \(\text{Arg}(z) = -5\pi/6\), whereas \(7\pi/6\) is a non-principal argument.

glossary.definition: De Moivre's formula states that for any angle \(\theta\) and any integer \(n\), \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\).
glossary.example: In Example 4 of §1.3, \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}i\right)^3 = \cos\frac{3\pi}{6} + i\sin\frac{3\pi}{6} = i\).

glossary.definition: An \(n\)th root of a nonzero complex number \(z\) is any complex number \(w\) satisfying \(w^n = z\), given for \(k = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1\) by Equation (4) of §1.4.
glossary.example: Every nonzero complex number \(z\) has exactly \(n\) distinct \(n\)th roots \(w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}\).

glossary.definition: The principal \(n\)th root of a nonzero complex number \(z\) is the unique root \(w_0\) obtained from the \(n\)th-root formula by taking \(\theta = \text{Arg}(z)\) and \(k = 0\).
glossary.example: In Example 1 of §1.4, since \(\text{Arg}(i) = \pi/2\), the principal cube root of \(i\) is \(w_0 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}i\).

glossary.definition: A neighborhood (or open disk) of \(z_0\) is the set of points satisfying \(|z - z_0| < \rho\), whereas \(|z - z_0| \le \rho\) is a closed disk and \(0 < |z - z_0| < \rho\) is a deleted neighborhood.
glossary.example: The inequality \(|z| < 1\) defines a neighborhood of the origin, and \(0 < |z| < 1\) defines a deleted neighborhood.

glossary.definition: A point \(z_0\) is an interior point of \(S\) if some neighborhood of \(z_0\) lies entirely within \(S\); \(S\) is an open set if every point of \(S\) is an interior point.
glossary.example: The right half-plane \(\text{Re}(z) > 1\) is an open set, whereas \(\text{Re}(z) \ge 1\) is not open.

glossary.definition: A point \(z_0\) is a boundary point of \(S\) if every neighborhood of \(z_0\) contains a point in \(S\) and a point not in \(S\); the set of all boundary points is the boundary of \(S\).
glossary.example: The circle \(|z - i| = 2\) is the boundary of both \(|z - i| \le 2\) and \(|z - i| < 2\).

glossary.definition: An open circular annulus centered at \(z_0\) is the open circular ring of points satisfying \(\rho_1 < |z - z_0| < \rho_2\) for \(0 < \rho_1 < \rho_2\).
glossary.example: In Figure 1.5.5(d), \(1 < |z| < 2\) is an open circular annulus centered at the origin.

glossary.definition: A set \(S\) is connected if any pair of points \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) in \(S\) can be joined by a polygonal line of finitely many line segments lying entirely inside \(S\).
glossary.example: The set \(\text{Re}(z) \neq 4\) is open but not connected because no polygonal line in the set can cross \(x = 4\).

glossary.definition: A domain in the complex plane is a set \(S\) that is both an open set and a connected set.
glossary.example: The open lower half-plane \(\text{Im}(z) < 0\) and the open ring \(1 < |z| < 2\) are both domains.

glossary.definition: A closed set is a set that contains all of its boundary points, while a region is a domain together with all, some, or none of its boundary points.
glossary.example: The closed disk \(|z - z_0| \le \rho\) is closed, whereas \(1 \le |z - 5| < 3\) is a region that is neither open nor closed.

glossary.definition: A set \(S\) is bounded if there exists a real number \(R > 0\) such that \(|z| < R\) for every \(z\) in \(S\); otherwise \(S\) is unbounded.
glossary.example: The annulus \(1 < |z| < 2\) is bounded, whereas the half-plane \(\text{Im}(z) < 0\) is unbounded.

glossary.definition: The Riemann sphere is the unit sphere \(x^2 + y^2 + u^2 = 1\) onto which the complex plane is mapped by stereographic projection from the north pole \((0, 0, 1)\), which represents \(\infty\).
glossary.example: Adjoining the ideal point at infinity \(\infty\) to \(\mathbf{C}\) gives the extended complex-number system.

cards.title: Extending real numbers with the imaginary unit i
cards.meaning: A complex number combines a real part a and an imaginary part b using the imaginary unit i, whose square is -1.

cards.picture: Each complex number z = a + ib pairs two real numbers a and b, with i² = -1.
cards.example: In z = 4 - 9i, the real part is 4 and the imaginary part is the real number -9, not -9i.
cards.bridge: Definition 1.1.1 and Definition 1.1.2 formalize complex numbers and when two of them are equal.

cards.title: What is a complex number?
cards.body: A complex number is any number \(z = a + ib\) where \(a = \text{Re}(z)\) and \(b = \text{Im}(z)\) are real numbers and the imaginary unit \(i\) satisfies \(i^2 = -1\).
cards.tex: z = a + ib, \quad i^2 = -1, \quad a = \text{Re}(z), \quad b = \text{Im}(z)

objects.text: Def. 1.1.1: z = a + ib with i² = -1
objects.name: realbox

cards.title: What is equality of complex numbers?
cards.body: Two complex numbers are equal if and only if their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal: \(a_1 = a_2\) and \(b_1 = b_2\).

cards.title: Why changing +ib to -ib turns multiplication into a real sum of squares
cards.meaning: The complex conjugate z̄ = a - ib reverses the sign of the imaginary part so that z and z̄ multiply to the real number a² + b².
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="20" y="34" width="96" height="46" class="s ok"/><rect x="144" y="34" width="96" height="46" class="s ok"/><line x1="68" y1="80" x2="122" y2="120" class="lk"/><line x1="192" y1="80" x2="138" y2="120" class="lk"/><rect x="58" y="120" width="144" height="40" class="f"/><text x="68" y="62" text-anchor="middle" class="t">z = a + ib</text><text x="192" y="62" text-anchor="middle" class="t">z̄ = a - ib</text><text x="130" y="144" text-anchor="middle" class="i">z z̄ = a² + b² (real)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Multiplying z = a + ib by its conjugate z̄ = a - ib cancels the cross terms and leaves a² + b².
cards.example: For z = 4 + 6i, the conjugate is z̄ = 4 - 6i and their product is 4² + 6² = 52.
cards.bridge: Equation (4) z z̄ = a² + b² allows us to divide complex numbers in Equation (7) by clearing i from the denominator.

cards.title: What is the complex conjugate?
cards.body: The complex conjugate of \(z = a + ib\) is \(\bar{z} = a - ib\), formed by changing the sign of the imaginary part so that \(z\bar{z} = a^2 + b^2\).

cards.title: What are inverses, and why is C not ordered?
cards.body: Every \(z\) has additive inverse \(-z\), every nonzero \(z\) has reciprocal \(z^{-1} = 1/z\), and \(\mathbf{C}\) has no order relation since \(i^2 = (-i)^2 = -1\).

objects.text: Prob. 55: no positive set P in C (i² = -1)
objects.name: order

cards.title: Example 2: Division using the conjugate (Equation (7))

phases.why: multiply numerator and denominator by z̄₂ = 4 - 6i

phases.name: Expand

steps.note: Start with \(z_1 = 2 - 3i\) and \(z_2 = 4 + 6i\) from Example 2.

ask.q: By Equation (7), what do we multiply top and bottom by?
ask.why: Equation (7) multiplies numerator and denominator by the conjugate z̄₂ = 4 - 6i of the denominator.

steps.note: Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\bar{z}_2 = 4 - 6i\).

ask.q: By Equation (4), what does the denominator \((4 + 6i)(4 - 6i)\) equal?
ask.why: By Equation (4), z₂z̄₂ = a₂² + b₂² = 4² + 6².

steps.note: Expand the numerator by the distributive law and write the denominator as \(4^2 + 6^2\).

ask.q: Since \(i^2 = -1\), what does \(8 - 12i - 12i + 18i^2\) simplify to?
ask.why: Replacing 18i² with -18 gives (8 - 18) + (-12 - 12)i = -10 - 24i.

ask.q: How do we write \(\frac{-10 - 24i}{52}\) in reduced \(a + bi\) form?
ask.why: Dividing both terms by 52 gives -10/52 - (24/52)i = -5/26 - (6/13)i.

steps.note: Divide the real and imaginary parts by \(52\) and reduce to lowest terms.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For the complex number \(z = 4 - 9i\), what is the imaginary part \(\text{Im}(z)\)?
cards.why: In z = a + ib, the imaginary part Im(z) is the real number b = -9, not -9i.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 1 of §1.1, what is the product \((2 + 4i)(-3 + 8i)\)?
cards.why: Using the distributive law and i² = -1 gives -6 + 16i - 12i + 32i² = -38 + 4i.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The number \(\bar{z} = a - ib\) obtained by changing the sign of \(\text{Im}(z)\) is the complex ______ of \(z\).
cards.why: Changing the sign of the imaginary part of z = a + ib gives its complex conjugate z̄ = a - ib.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: By Equation (4) of §1.1, what is the value of \(z\bar{z}\) when \(z = 2 - 3i\)?
cards.why: By Equation (4), z z̄ = a² + b² = 2² + (-3)² = 4 + 9 = 13.

cards.title: Viewing a complex number as a point and a position vector
cards.meaning: Every complex number z = x + iy sits at (x, y) in the complex plane at distance |z| = √(x² + y²) from the origin.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="24" y1="138" x2="236" y2="138" class="ik"/><line x1="64" y1="162" x2="64" y2="20" class="ik"/><line x1="64" y1="138" x2="184" y2="54" class="lk"/><line x1="184" y1="138" x2="184" y2="54" class="gk"/><circle cx="184" cy="54" r="4" class="f"/><text x="188" y="44" class="t">z = x + iy (x, y)</text><text x="112" y="84" class="t">|z| = √(x²+y²)</text><text x="124" y="154" text-anchor="middle" class="t">x</text><text x="198" y="98" class="t">y</text><text x="222" y="154" class="t">Real</text><text x="88" y="30" class="t">Imaginary</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Figure 1.2.2: the right triangle with legs x and y has hypotenuse |z| = √(x² + y²).
cards.example: For z = 2 - 3i at (2, -3), the distance from the origin is |z| = √(2² + (-3)²) = √13.
cards.bridge: Definition 1.2.1 calls this distance the modulus (or absolute value) of z.

cards.title: What are the complex plane and the modulus of z?
cards.body: The complex plane plots \(z = x + iy\) at \((x, y)\), and the modulus \(|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) is the distance from the origin to \((x, y)\).

cards.title: What is the distance between two points in the complex plane?
cards.body: The distance between two points \(z_1 = x_1 + iy_1\) and \(z_2 = x_2 + iy_2\) in the complex plane is the modulus of their difference, \(|z_2 - z_1|\).

cards.title: What is the triangle inequality?
cards.body: The triangle inequality states that the modulus of a sum \(|z_1 + z_2|\) is at most \(|z_1| + |z_2|\) and at least \(\big||z_1| - |z_2|\big|\).

cards.label: Example 2 · §1.2
cards.title: Example 2: Set of points satisfying |z| = |z - i|
cards.legend: \(z = x + iy\) point in the plane, \(|z|\) distance to \(0\), \(|z - i|\) distance to \(i\).

phases.name: Distance formula
phases.why: write |z| and |z - i| in terms of x and y

phases.name: Square both sides
phases.why: remove the square roots and expand (y - 1)²

phases.name: Cancel squares
phases.why: subtract x² + y² from both sides

phases.name: Solve for y
phases.why: isolate y to identify the horizontal line

steps.note: Start from the given condition that \(z\) is equidistant from \(0\) and \(i\).

ask.q: Using \(z = x + iy\) and Equations (1) and (5), how is \(|z| = |z - i|\) written?
ask.why: Since z - i = x + i(y - 1), Equations (1) and (5) give √(x² + y²) = √(x² + (y - 1)²).

steps.note: Express both moduli in terms of the real coordinates \(x\) and \(y\).

ask.q: What is the first algebra move to remove the square roots?
ask.why: Squaring both non-negative sides removes the radical signs cleanly.

steps.note: Square both sides of the equation.

ask.q: What do we get when we expand \((y - 1)^2\) on the right-hand side?
ask.why: Expanding the binomial square gives (y - 1)² = y² - 2y + 1.

steps.note: Expand \((y - 1)^2 = y^2 - 2y + 1\) on the right.

ask.q: After subtracting \(x^2 + y^2\) and solving for \(y\), what line do we obtain?
ask.why: Canceling x² + y² leaves 0 = -2y + 1, so 2y = 1 and y = 1/2.

steps.note: Subtract \(x^2 + y^2\) from both sides.
The locus is the horizontal line \(y = \frac{1}{2}\), or \(z = x + \frac{1}{2}i\) (Figure 1.2.4).

cards.label: Example 3 · §1.2
cards.title: Example 3: Upper bound for |-1 / (z⁴ + 3z² + 2)| when |z| = 2
cards.legend: \(|z| = 2\) circle of radius 2, \(M\) upper bound on the modulus of the fraction.

phases.name: Factor denominator
phases.why: write z⁴ + 3z² + 2 as (z² + 1)(z² + 2)

phases.name: Reverse triangle inequality
phases.why: apply Equation (8) to each factor in Equation (12)

phases.name: Evaluate at |z| = 2
phases.why: use |z²| = |z|² = 4 to find the minimum denominator

phases.name: Reciprocal bound
phases.why: take the reciprocal to get the upper bound 1/6

steps.note: Factor the quadratic in \(z^2\) inside the denominator modulus.

ask.q: By the product property in Equation (3), how does \(|(z^2 + 1)(z^2 + 2)|\) split?
ask.why: By Equation (3), the modulus of a product equals the product of the moduli: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.

steps.note: Use Equation (3) to write the product of two moduli.

ask.q: By Equation (8), what is the lower bound for each factor \(|z^2 + c|\)?
ask.why: Equation (8) states that |z₁ + z₂| ≥ ||z₁| - |z₂||, giving Equation (12).

steps.note: By Equation (12) and \(|z^2| = |z|^2\), the denominator is at least \(L\).

ask.q: When \(|z| = 2\), what is the value of \(L = \big||z|^2 - 1\big| \cdot \big||z|^2 - 2\big|\)?
ask.why: Substituting |z| = 2 gives |4 - 1| · |4 - 2| = 3 · 2 = 6.

steps.note: Substitute \(|z|^2 = 2^2 = 4\) into both factors.
Since \(|z^4 + 3z^2 + 2| \ge L = 6\), the denominator is at least \(6\).

ask.q: Since \(|z^4 + 3z^2 + 2| \ge 6\) and \(|-1| = 1\), what is the upper bound \(M\)?
ask.why: Taking the reciprocal reverses the inequality: 1 / |z⁴ + 3z² + 2| ≤ 1/6.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 2 of §1.2, what set of points satisfies \(|z| = |z - i|\)?
cards.why: Points equidistant from 0 and i lie on the perpendicular bisector, the horizontal line y = 1/2.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which inequality is given in Equation (8) of §1.2 for any \(z_1, z_2\)?
cards.why: Equation (8) states the reverse triangle inequality ||z₁| - |z₂|| ≤ |z₁ + z₂|.

cards.q: The inequality \(|z_1 + z_2| \le |z_1| + |z_2|\) in Equation (6) is called the ______ inequality.
cards.why: Equation (6) is the triangle inequality, expressing that one side of a triangle cannot exceed the sum of the other two sides.

cards.title: Locating z by its distance r and angle θ from the positive real axis
cards.meaning: Instead of rectangular coordinates (x, y), polar form uses the modulus r = |z| and the radian angle θ = arg(z).

cards.picture: Look at Figure 1.3.2: substituting x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ into x + iy gives r(cos θ + i sin θ).
cards.example: For z = -√3 - i in Quadrant III, r = 2 and θ = 7π/6 (or principal argument Arg(z) = -5π/6).
cards.bridge: Polar form turns complex multiplication, division, and integer powers into simple angle addition and scaling.

cards.title: What are the polar form and argument of a complex number?
cards.body: The polar form of a nonzero complex number \(z = x + iy\) is \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), where \(r = |z|\) and \(\theta = \arg(z)\) is the angle in radians.
cards.tex: z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta), \qquad x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad r = |z|

objects.text: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)
objects.name: pt

cards.title: What is the principal argument Arg(z)?
cards.body: The principal argument \(\text{Arg}(z)\) is the unique value of \(\arg(z)\) that lies in the interval \(-\pi < \text{Arg}(z) \le \pi\).

cards.title: What is de Moivre's formula, and how do polar products work?
cards.body: Polar multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments, yielding integer powers \(z^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)\) and de Moivre's formula for \(r = 1\).
cards.tex: z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2[\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2) + i\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)], \quad (\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta

cards.title: Polar multiplication, integer powers, and de Moivre's formula

phases.name: Addition formulas
phases.why: apply cosine and sine addition identities to get Equation (6)

phases.why: repeat multiplication n times for z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)

phases.name: de Moivre's formula
phases.why: set r = 1 on the unit circle to obtain Equation (10)

steps.note: Write both complex numbers in polar form and multiply them.

ask.q: When we expand the product and use \(i^2 = -1\), what is the real part inside the bracket?
ask.why: Since (i sin θ₁)(i sin θ₂) = -sin θ₁ sin θ₂, the real part in Equation (4) is cos θ₁ cos θ₂ - sin θ₁ sin θ₂.

steps.note: Equation (4): group the real terms and the imaginary terms.

ask.q: By the trigonometric addition formulas, how does Equation (4) simplify?
ask.why: The cosine and sine addition formulas turn Equation (4) into Equation (6) with angle θ₁ + θ₂.

steps.note: Equation (6): lengths multiply (\(r_1 r_2\)) and arguments add (\(\theta_1 + \theta_2\)).

ask.q: Setting \(z_1 = z_2 = z\) and repeating \(n\) times gives which formula in Equation (9)?
ask.why: Multiplying z by itself n times raises r to the nth power and adds θ to itself n times, giving Equation (9).

steps.note: Equation (9) holds for any integer \(n\) (including negative integers via Equation (7)).

ask.q: When \(z = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\) so that \(r = 1\), what does Equation (9) yield?
ask.why: Setting r = 1 in Equation (9) gives de Moivre's formula in Equation (10).

steps.note: Equation (10): de Moivre's formula for any integer \(n\).

cards.label: Example 3 · §1.3
cards.title: Examples 1 & 3: Polar form and cube of z = -√3 - i

phases.name: Modulus & angle
phases.why: find r = 2 and θ = 7π/6 in the third quadrant

phases.name: Apply Equation (9)
phases.why: raise r to power 3 and multiply θ by 3

phases.name: Simplify angle
phases.why: reduce 3(7π/6) = 7π/2

phases.name: Rectangular form
phases.why: evaluate cos(7π/2) = 0 and sin(7π/2) = -1

steps.note: From Example 1 (Equation (2)), \(z = -\sqrt{3} - i\) has \(r = 2\) and \(\theta = 7\pi/6\).

ask.q: In Example 1, why did we add \(\pi\) to \(\tan^{-1}(1/\sqrt{3}) = \pi/6\)?
options: Because \(-\sqrt{3} - i\) is in Quadrant III
Because \(-\sqrt{3} - i\) is in Quadrant II
ask.why: Since x = -√3 < 0 and y = -1 < 0, the point lies in the third quadrant, so θ = π/6 + π = 7π/6.

steps.note: Apply Equation (9) with \(r = 2\), \(\theta = 7\pi/6\), and \(n = 3\).

ask.q: What do \(2^3\) and \(3 \cdot \frac{7\pi}{6}\) simplify to?
ask.why: We have 2³ = 8 and 3 · (7π/6) = 7π/2.

ask.q: What are the values of \(\cos(7\pi/2)\) and \(\sin(7\pi/2)\)?
ask.why: Since 7π/2 = 2π + 3π/2, cos(7π/2) = cos(3π/2) = 0 and sin(7π/2) = sin(3π/2) = -1.

steps.note: Substitute \(\cos(7\pi/2) = 0\) and \(\sin(7\pi/2) = -1\).

ask.q: What is the final value of \((-\sqrt{3} - i)^3\) in Example 3?
ask.why: Multiplying 8 by -i gives z³ = -8i.

steps.note: Example 3 complete: \((-\sqrt{3} - i)^3 = -8i\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which interval defines the principal argument \(\text{Arg}(z)\) in §1.3?
cards.why: In §1.3, the principal argument Arg(z) is the unique argument in the interval -π < Arg(z) ≤ π.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the principal argument \(\text{Arg}(z)\) of \(z = -\sqrt{3} - i\)?
cards.why: As shown in Figure 1.3.5, the unique angle of -√3 - i in (-π, π] is π/6 - π = -5π/6.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Example 4 of §1.3, what is \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}i\right)^3\)?
cards.why: With θ = π/6, de Moivre's formula gives cos(3π/6) + i sin(3π/6) = cos(π/2) + i sin(π/2) = i.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Equation (10), \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\), is known as ______ formula.
cards.answer: de Moivre's|de Moivre|De Moivre's|de Moivre's formula
cards.why: Setting r = 1 in Equation (9) gives de Moivre's formula, Equation (10).

cards.title: Why every nonzero complex number has n equally spaced nth roots
cards.meaning: Solving wⁿ = z takes the positive nth root of the modulus r and divides the angles θ + 2kπ by n, placing n roots evenly around a circle.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="24" y1="90" x2="236" y2="90" class="ik"/><line x1="130" y1="168" x2="130" y2="12" class="ik"/><circle cx="130" cy="90" r="56" class="s ok"/><line x1="130" y1="90" x2="178" y2="62" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="90" x2="82" y2="62" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="90" x2="130" y2="146" class="lk"/><circle cx="178" cy="62" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="82" cy="62" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="130" cy="146" r="4" class="f"/><text x="204" y="58" text-anchor="middle" class="t">w₀ (π/6)</text><text x="56" y="58" text-anchor="middle" class="t">w₁ (5π/6)</text><text x="162" y="154" text-anchor="middle" class="t">w₂ = -i</text><text x="130" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Fig. 1.4.1: Cube roots of i</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Figure 1.4.1: the three cube roots of i sit on the unit circle separated by 2π/3 radians.
cards.example: For z = i, the three cube roots are w₀ = √3/2 + i/2, w₁ = -√3/2 + i/2, and w₂ = -i.
cards.bridge: Equation (4) of §1.4 gives all n distinct nth roots w_k for k = 0, 1, ..., n - 1.

cards.title: What are the nth roots of a nonzero complex number?
cards.body: A complex number \(w\) is an \(n\)th root of a nonzero complex number \(z\) if \(w^n = z\), which has \(n\) distinct solutions \(w_0, w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}\).

cards.title: What is the principal nth root, and how are roots spaced?
cards.body: The principal \(n\)th root \(w_0\) uses \(\theta = \text{Arg}(z)\) and \(k = 0\), while all \(n\) roots sit spaced by \(2\pi/n\) on the circle of radius \(\sqrt[n]{r}\).

cards.label: Derivation · §1.4
cards.title: Formula for the n nth roots of z (Equations (1)–(4))
cards.legend: \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\) given nonzero number, \(w = \rho(\cos\phi + i\sin\phi)\) unknown \(n\)th root.

phases.name: Polar equation
phases.why: write wⁿ = z in polar form using Equation (9) of §1.3

phases.name: Match moduli
phases.why: equate the positive moduli ρⁿ = r to find ρ

phases.name: Match arguments
phases.why: equate cos nφ = cos θ and sin nφ = sin θ

phases.name: Distinct roots
phases.why: substitute ρ and φ for k = 0, 1, ..., n - 1 into w

steps.note: Equation (1): express \(w^n = z\) using polar forms \(w = \rho(\cos\phi + i\sin\phi)\) and \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\).

ask.q: Comparing the moduli of both sides of Equation (1) gives which equation?
ask.why: Since both cos nφ + i sin nφ and cos θ + i sin θ have modulus 1, equating moduli gives ρⁿ = r (Equation (2)).

steps.note: Equation (2): the positive modulus \(\rho\) of \(w\) satisfies \(\rho^n = r\).

ask.q: Since \(\rho\) and \(r\) are positive real numbers, what is \(\rho\)?
ask.why: We define ρ = ⁿ√r to be the unique positive nth root of the positive real number r.

steps.note: All \(n\) roots lie on the circle of radius \(\rho = \sqrt[n]{r}\) centered at the origin.

ask.q: From \(\cos n\phi = \cos\theta\) and \(\sin n\phi = \sin\theta\), how are \(n\phi\) and \(\theta\) related?
ask.why: Because cosine and sine have period 2π, nφ and θ can differ by any integer multiple 2kπ.

steps.note: Equating real and imaginary parts in Equation (3) relates \(n\phi\) and \(\theta\) up to \(2k\pi\).
Divide both sides by \(n\) to find the argument \(\phi\) of each root.

ask.q: Which integer values of \(k\) produce all \(n\) distinct \(n\)th roots of \(z\)?
ask.why: As k runs through 0, 1, 2, ..., n - 1 we get n distinct roots; for k ≥ n the angles repeat modulo 2π.

steps.note: Equation (4): for \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, n - 1\), this gives the \(n\) distinct \(n\)th roots of \(z\).

cards.label: Example 1 · §1.4
cards.title: Example 1: Finding the three cube roots of z = i
cards.legend: \(z = i\) with \(r = 1\) and \(\theta = \text{Arg}(i) = \pi/2\), \(n = 3\), \(w_0, w_1, w_2\) cube roots.

phases.name: Polar setup
phases.why: write z = i with r = 1, θ = π/2, and n = 3 in Equation (4)

phases.name: k = 0 (principal)
phases.why: evaluate w₀ at angle (π/2)/3 = π/6

phases.name: k = 1
phases.why: evaluate w₁ at angle (π/2 + 2π)/3 = 5π/6

phases.name: k = 2
phases.why: evaluate w₂ at angle (π/2 + 4π)/3 = 3π/2

steps.note: Substitute \(r = 1\), \(\theta = \pi/2\), and \(n = 3\) into Equation (4) for \(k = 0, 1, 2\).

ask.q: For \(k = 0\), what is the angle \(\frac{\pi/2 + 0}{3}\) of the principal cube root \(w_0\)?
ask.why: Dividing π/2 by 3 gives the principal root angle π/6.

steps.note: Set \(k = 0\) to obtain the principal cube root \(w_0\).

ask.q: What is \(w_0 = \cos(\pi/6) + i\sin(\pi/6)\) in \(a + bi\) form?
ask.why: Since cos(π/6) = √3/2 and sin(π/6) = 1/2, we get w₀ = √3/2 + (1/2)i.

steps.note: This is the principal cube root of \(i\).

ask.q: For \(k = 1\), the angle is \(\frac{\pi/2 + 2\pi}{3} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\). What is \(w_1\)?
ask.why: At 5π/6 in Quadrant II, cos(5π/6) = -√3/2 and sin(5π/6) = 1/2.

ask.q: For \(k = 2\), the angle is \(\frac{\pi/2 + 4\pi}{3} = \frac{3\pi}{2}\). What is \(w_2\)?
ask.why: Since cos(3π/2) = 0 and sin(3π/2) = -1, the third cube root is w₂ = -i.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 1 of §1.4, which number is the principal cube root of \(z = i\)?
cards.why: Using Arg(i) = π/2 and k = 0 gives the principal cube root w₀ = cos(π/6) + i sin(π/6) = √3/2 + (1/2)i.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the radian angle between any two successive \(n\)th roots \(w_k\) and \(w_{k+1}\)?
cards.why: The arguments of w_k and w_{k+1} differ by [(θ + 2(k+1)π) - (θ + 2kπ)] / n = 2π/n.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many distinct fourth roots does the complex number \(z = 1 + i\) have?
cards.why: Every nonzero complex number has exactly n distinct nth roots, so 1 + i has 4 distinct fourth roots.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The unique root \(w_0\) found using \(\theta = \text{Arg}(z)\) and \(k = 0\) is the ______ \(n\)th root of \(z\).
cards.why: In §1.4, choosing θ = Arg(z) and k = 0 in Equation (4) defines the principal nth root of z.

sheets.title: Sets of Points in the Complex Plane

cards.title: From a circle of radius ρ to open neighborhoods and rings
cards.meaning: Because |z - z₀| is the distance from z₀ to z, |z - z₀| = ρ is a circle and |z - z₀| < ρ is the open disk (neighborhood) inside it.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="74" cy="92" r="44" class="s ok"/><circle cx="74" cy="92" r="3.5" class="f"/><line x1="74" y1="92" x2="112" y2="70" class="lk"/><circle cx="190" cy="92" r="44" class="s"/><circle cx="190" cy="92" r="44" class="gk"/><circle cx="190" cy="92" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="74" y="108" text-anchor="middle" class="t">z₀</text><text x="98" y="76" class="t">ρ</text><text x="74" y="154" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Disk |z - z₀| ≤ ρ</text><text x="190" y="108" text-anchor="middle" class="t">z₀</text><text x="190" y="154" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Neighborhood |z - z₀| < ρ</text><text x="130" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Solid boundary (included) vs. dashed boundary (excluded)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Including the circle |z - z₀| = ρ gives a closed disk; excluding the circle gives an open neighborhood of z₀.
cards.example: The inequality |z| < 1 is a neighborhood of the origin, and 0 < |z| < 1 is a deleted neighborhood that also removes 0.
cards.bridge: Neighborhoods let us test whether every point of a set S has breathing room inside S, defining open sets and domains.

cards.title: What are circles, disks, neighborhoods, and annuli?
cards.body: For \(\rho > 0\), \(|z - z_0| = \rho\) is a circle, \(|z - z_0| \le \rho\) is a closed disk, \(|z - z_0| < \rho\) is a neighborhood, and \(\rho_1 < |z - z_0| < \rho_2\) is an annulus.

cards.title: What are interior points, open sets, and boundary points?
cards.body: A set \(S\) is open if every point of \(S\) has a neighborhood entirely inside \(S\), while boundary points have every neighborhood meeting both \(S\) and its complement.
cards.tex: \text{Re}(z) > 1 \text{ (open set)}, \qquad \text{boundary of } |z - i| \le 2 \text{ and } |z - i| < 2 \text{ is } |z - i| = 2

cards.title: What are connected sets, domains, closed sets, and bounded sets?
cards.body: A set is connected if polygonal lines inside it join any two points, a domain is an open connected set, a closed set holds all its boundary, and a bounded set fits in \(|z| < R\).
cards.tex: \text{Domain} = \text{open} + \text{connected}, \qquad S \text{ bounded} \iff |z| < R \text{ for all } z \in S

cards.title: What are the Riemann sphere and the point at infinity?
cards.body: Stereographic projection maps each \(z\) in the plane onto the unit Riemann sphere and identifies the north pole \((0, 0, 1)\) with the point at infinity \(\infty\).

cards.label: Example 1 · §1.5
cards.title: Example 1(b) & Open Half-Plane: Circle center and interior neighborhood
cards.legend: \(z = x + iy\), \(z_0 = 1 - 3i\) circle center, \(\rho = 5\) circle radius, \(\varepsilon\) neighborhood radius.

phases.name: Group center z₀
phases.why: rewrite |z - 1 + 3i| = 5 in standard form |z - z₀| = ρ

phases.name: Read center & radius
phases.why: match with Equation (1) to identify z₀ and ρ

phases.name: Half-plane point
phases.why: check distance from z₁ = 1.1 + 2i to boundary x = 1

phases.name: Interior neighborhood
phases.why: choose radius ε = 0.05 < 0.1 so the neighborhood stays in Re(z) > 1

steps.note: Start with the circle equation in Example 1(b) of §1.5.

ask.q: To match Equation (1), \(|z - z_0| = \rho\), how do we rewrite \(|z - 1 + 3i|\)?
ask.why: Factoring a minus sign out of -1 + 3i gives -(1 - 3i), so |z - 1 + 3i| = |z - (1 - 3i)|.

steps.note: Write \(z - 1 + 3i\) in the standard form \(z - z_0\).

ask.q: From \(|z - (1 - 3i)| = 5\), what is the center \(z_0\) of the circle?
ask.why: Comparing |z - (1 - 3i)| = 5 with Equation (1) |z - z₀| = ρ gives center z₀ = 1 - 3i and radius ρ = 5.

steps.note: Example 1(b): the equation describes a circle of radius \(\rho = 5\) centered at \(z_0 = 1 - 3i\).

ask.q: In Figure 1.5.3, how far is \(z_1 = 1.1 + 2i\) from the boundary line \(x = 1\) of \(\text{Re}(z) > 1\)?
ask.why: Since Re(1.1 + 2i) = 1.1, the horizontal distance to the vertical line x = 1 is 1.1 - 1 = 0.1.

steps.note: Measure the distance \(d = 0.1\) from \(z_1 = 1.1 + 2i\) to the boundary line \(x = 1\).

ask.q: Which neighborhood radius \(\varepsilon\) in Figure 1.5.3 lies entirely inside \(\text{Re}(z) > 1\)?
ask.why: Any radius smaller than 0.1 works; Figure 1.5.3 chooses ε = 0.05 so |z - (1.1 + 2i)| < 0.05 lies entirely in Re(z) > 1.

steps.note: Thus \(|z - (1.1 + 2i)| < 0.05\) lies entirely in \(\text{Re}(z) > 1\), showing \(1.1 + 2i\) is an interior point.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 1(b) of §1.5, what are the center and radius of \(|z - 1 + 3i| = 5\)?
cards.why: Rewriting |z - 1 + 3i| = 5 as |z - (1 - 3i)| = 5 shows the center is z₀ = 1 - 3i and the radius is 5.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which two properties define a domain \(S\) in the complex plane?
cards.why: In §1.5, an open connected set in the complex plane is called a domain.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How is the annular region \(1 \le |z - 5| < 3\) classified in §1.5?
cards.why: Because 1 ≤ |z - 5| < 3 contains its inner boundary circle |z - 5| = 1 but not its outer boundary circle |z - 5| = 3, it is neither open nor closed.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In §1.5, an open connected set in the complex plane is called a ______.
cards.why: By definition in §1.5, a set that is both open and connected is called a domain.
